content: Prepatellar bursitis, also referred to as housemaid's knee, is a condition characterized by swelling and pain localized above the kneecap (patella). This condition arises due to inflammation of the prepatellar bursa, a superficial structure with a thin synovial lining that lies between the skin and the patella. Its primary function is to reduce friction over the underlying structures and facilitate an optimal range of motion in the knee joint. Aseptic prepatellar bursitis, the most common form, is frequently caused by repetitive kneeling activities, which explains its colloquial name, housemaid's knee. Inflammation of the prepatellar bursa can be classified as either aseptic (non-infectious) or septic (infectious, such as bacterial in origin). Septic prepatellar bursitis is more prevalent in children and individuals with compromised immune systems. Statistically, this condition is more commonly observed in men than in women. Physical Examination Findings: In cases of prepatellar bursitis caused by bacterial infection, there is visible redness and swelling of the prepatellar bursa. Inflammation and fluid accumulation (edema) may lead to skin peeling (desquamation). Severe bacterial infections of the prepatellar bursa can result in extensive redness and swelling. In contrast, infrapatellar bursitis, which involves the bursa located below the patella, also presents with redness and swelling, but it affects a different anatomical region. Differential Diagnosis: It is essential to distinguish prepatellar bursitis from other types of bursitis or conditions that may present with similar symptoms. Treatment: In more complex cases, oral nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) or corticosteroid injections may be administered, provided that an infection has been excluded. Surgical excision of the bursa is rarely required. However, if acute bursitis is not properly addressed, it may progress to a chronic condition.
